content: Providing TB preventive treatment (TPT) to household contacts can yield substantial benefits, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), where the prevalence of TB infection often exceeds 50%. Systematic reviews indicate that the prevalence of active TB disease among household contacts in LMICs ranges from 3% to 5%. The PHOENIx Feasibility Study, conducted across eight high TB-burden countries, revealed that systematic household contact investigations among 1,007 contacts of 284 patients with multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) identified new TB disease in 12% of contacts. Additionally, 72% of these contacts were found to have TB infection, as determined by positive tuberculin skin tests (TST) or interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA). Consequently, screening household contacts for TB disease is a high-priority, cost-effective strategy for TB control programs, as it enables early detection and treatment of TB disease and infection, thereby reducing transmission and improving outcomes. Investigating and treating all household contacts not only prevents TB transmission but also mitigates the severe social and economic consequences of TB, such as catastrophic healthcare costs and loss of income. A holistic family health approach, which includes offering TPT to all family members while the index TB patient is still receiving treatment, enhances the understanding and impact of TPT and improves cost-effectiveness through interventions like home visits. Strengthening contact investigation programs is essential to achieving global commitments, such as providing TPT to 24 million household contacts by 2022. Contact investigation is a systematic process to identify individuals with TB disease and those who require TPT. It involves identifying contacts, conducting clinical evaluations or testing, and providing appropriate anti-TB therapy or TPT. This process should be a standard component of national TB control efforts and is critical for tracking infectious diseases like TB and COVID-19. Ministries of health should invest in strengthening health system capacity to conduct contact investigations, ensuring coverage for all age groups, and dedicating necessary resources to establish effective mechanisms. Key steps in contact investigation include reviewing index patient information, assessing the degree of infectiousness, counseling the index patient, enumerating household and close contacts, and developing a plan for investigation. Home visits or health center evaluations should be conducted, followed by clinical assessments, testing, and treatment for TB disease or TPT as appropriate. Ruling out active TB disease before initiating TPT is a critical step to prevent delays in treatment and the emergence of drug resistance. This process involves screening for TB symptoms, conducting diagnostic tests, and using chest radiography when available. For people living with HIV (PLHIV), symptom screening alone has high sensitivity and negative predictive value, making it a reliable method to rule out TB disease. Chest radiography can enhance diagnostic confidence but should not be a mandatory requirement, as it may create barriers to TPT access. Governments and donors should invest in scaling up access to chest radiography and other diagnostic tools while ensuring that lack of access does not hinder TPT implementation. Ministries of health should coordinate activities to screen for and exclude TB disease as part of comprehensive care packages for at-risk populations. This includes developing national guidelines, training healthcare workers, and integrating TB screening into existing health services. Communication materials and job aids should be made available at all service delivery sites to support intensified TB screening efforts. In summary, systematic contact investigation and the provision of TPT are essential strategies to reduce TB transmission, improve health outcomes, and achieve global TB control targets. Strengthening health systems, ensuring adequate resources, and integrating TB prevention into broader healthcare services are critical to the success of these efforts.
